newsitem.title: UK: BOE says studying bonus impact on financial risk.
newsitem.headline: BOE says studying bonus impact on financial risk.

text.p: Bank of England deputy governor Howard Davies said the Bank was studying the impact of bonus schemes on financial risk in order to see whether there were any regulatory implications.

"Clearly moral hazard is an important issue. But a parallel question is whether the incentives for individuals within firms exacerbate risks," Davies told an annual "Money Macro and Finance' conference organised by the London Business School.
Davies said the Bank's study was looking at how financial firms actually determine their compensation packages and was considering the implications.

"Different methods of calculating bonuses can create different incentives with regard to individual traders. In particular, poorly designed schemes could create incentives for individuals to take exposures which are not in the interests of the firm," Davies said.
Davies said the Bank was intensifying research into banking regulation and was trying to form closer ties with academics.
"Research now needs to move into new areas such as how models could be built to encompass credit risk as well as market risk. We are currently carrying out some work in that area," he said.

Davies said much of the research carried out in the past by the BOE on regulation had not been published, but it would take a more open approach to this in the future, making more material available to researchers working outside the Bank.

The Bank was boosting its research into wider regulatory questions and the changing nature of systemic risk, viewed in terms of problems in the banking sector when the failure of one bank leads to a wider collapse in confidence, Davies said.
A key question was whether developments in the industry had substantially changed this risk or the risk of other types of contagion, as in through direct exposure between firms, he said.

That question fell into three parts, Davies said. The first was whether the risk of a bank failing was now substantially changed, through developments such as greater diversification across product ranges, or better hedging and risk control.
Offsetting this were internal control issues such as the complexity of firms and the speed with which new instruments enabled exposures to be built up, he noted.
"Overall it is not clear that the banks are carrying smaller exposures than was the case...," he said.
The second part of the question was whether th risks of contagion between banks had changed, Davies said.
The development of a Real Time Gross Settlement system had not altered exposures between many banks and other players.
"The third issue is whether the links between the banks and the real economy are now looser, which would reduce the systemic impact of any problems," Davies said.
"Here our current view is that the banks' role in the payments system and as a prime home for transactions balances continues to make them a fundamental part of the functioning of the real economy."
